opus-5.5.text:
Tri is a great example because he doesn't fit neatly into the old categories. For a long time the picture of a successful ML PhD student was someone who's very good at math or modeling, comes up with a clever new architecture or loss function, and runs experiments on top of whatever infrastructure exists. Tri works across the whole stack. FlashAttention isn't a new model. It's the observation that the bottleneck in attention isn't really the FLOPs, it's memory movement on the GPU. To see that, you have to understand the hardware: the memory hierarchy, how SRAM and HBM interact, what a kernel actually does. Then you need the algorithmic sense to restructure the computation, with tiling and recomputation, so it's exact but IO-aware.

The skill I'd point to is being willing to go down a level of abstraction when the abstraction is what's holding you back. Many of us, myself included, were trained to treat PyTorch as the floor. Tri treats it as one layer among many. When something is slow or seems impossible, he asks why at the systems level, not just the modeling level.

The other piece is that he connects that systems work back to modeling questions. The state space model work with Mamba is partly a modeling idea and partly a statement about what can run efficiently on modern hardware. Those two things are deeply entangled now, and the people making the biggest contributions understand both sides.

So for a graduate student today, my advice would be not to outsource your understanding of the hardware. Learn how GPUs work. Write a kernel, even a bad one. Know where the time actually goes. It's no longer a niche engineering skill. It's increasingly central to having good research ideas, because what's possible in this field is so tightly coupled to what's efficient.

It's also a lesson about taste. Tri picks problems where a real, practical bottleneck meets a clean underlying idea. That combination is rare, and it's why his work gets adopted so widely, so quickly.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes learning GPU hardware and writing kernels, while describing Tri’s habit of asking why and pursuing underlying ideas. It connects that combination to developing strong research ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
Tri is a great example because he didn't pick a lane. If you look at the FlashAttention work, the core idea isn't really a deep learning idea at all. It's a systems idea about memory hierarchy, about the fact that moving data between high-bandwidth memory and SRAM is the real bottleneck, not the FLOPs. And then he had the skills to actually go write the CUDA kernels, benchmark them honestly, and ship something people could pip install. That combination is rare. Most grad students end up either as the person who proves the theorem or the person who runs the experiments, and he's comfortable at the math level, the algorithms level, and the hardware level all at once.

The second thing I'd point to is that he picked the right problem. Attention being quadratic was something everyone knew about and everyone was trying to fix with approximations, sparse patterns, low-rank tricks. His move was to say, maybe the exact computation is fine, we're just doing it badly. That's a kind of taste, noticing that the field has collectively accepted a framing and asking whether the framing is actually the problem.

And then with Mamba and the state space work, you see the same pattern. There's a theoretical thread back to classical signal processing, there's a hardware-aware implementation, and there's a willingness to go against the consensus that transformers are the end of the story.

So if I were advising a student, I'd say: learn the stack below the one you think you work at. If you do modeling, understand the systems. If you do systems, understand the math. And spend real time on the implementation, because the ideas that win are the ones that actually run fast.

r001.rationale: The response highlights hands-on low-level systems and hardware expertise alongside curiosity and taste in questioning accepted framings and exploring ideas.

astra-6.text:
I think Tri exemplifies this combination of really understanding the mathematical ideas and being able to make them work efficiently on actual hardware. Those are often treated as separate skills: you come up with an algorithm, and then somebody else implements it. But with something like FlashAttention, the implementation constraints are central to the algorithm itself.

For a graduate student, that’s a powerful way to approach research. You want to be able to move between levels—to understand the model, look at what the computation is doing, and ask where the real bottleneck is. You don’t have to be an expert in everything, but being able to connect those pieces can let you make contributions that a lot of other researchers can build on.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes connecting mathematical ideas with efficient hardware implementation, but it does not clearly identify curiosity-driven exploration of ideas as an important skill.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Tri exemplifies this combination of really understanding the mathematical side of a problem and being able to make it work incredibly well on actual hardware. With FlashAttention, you have to understand attention, but you also have to understand where the data moves, how GPU memory works, and what actually makes an implementation fast. Those aren’t separate questions—the systems constraints help you see the algorithm differently.

For a graduate student, I think that’s a really powerful skill to develop: being able to move between those levels. You can have a great idea, implement it, measure it, and then use what you learn from the implementation to improve the idea. You don’t have to be an expert in everything, but being willing to go all the way down into the details can open up research directions you wouldn’t see otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response pairs deep understanding of GPU hardware and implementation details with developing and improving ideas through implementation and measurement, noting that this can reveal new research directions.
